title: Apply fertilizers to ornamental plants and landscapes

lessons.title: What fertiliser is
lessons.html:
What fertiliser is

Plants need food to grow. They take food from the soil through their roots. Over time the soil runs out of food. Fertiliser puts food back into the soil.

Main plant foods

FoodLetterWhat it does
NitrogenNGreen leaves and growth
PhosphorusPStrong roots and flowers
PotassiumKHealthy plants, good flowers and fruit

A fertiliser bag shows numbers like 2:3:2 or 3:1:5. These tell you how much N, P and K are in it, in that order.

Types of fertiliser

  • Granules: small hard balls that you spread on the soil. Example: lawn fertiliser.
  • Liquid or soluble: you mix it with water and pour or spray it. It works fast.
  • Slow-release: feeds the plant slowly for months. Often used in nursery pots.
  • Organic: from animals or plants, like kraal manure, chicken manure pellets, bone meal and compost.

Signs a plant needs food

  • Pale or yellow leaves
  • Slow growth
  • Few flowers
  • Thin, weak lawn

Yellow leaves can also come from too much water or pests. Ask your team leader before you feed.

Too much is bad

Too much fertiliser burns roots and leaves. The leaves go brown at the edges and the plant can die. Extra fertiliser also washes into rivers and dams and pollutes the water.

That is why we always use the right amount, at the right time. Most plants are fed in spring and summer, when they grow. Your team leader will make a feeding plan for each garden or nursery block. Follow the plan and write down what you used and where.

lessons.title: Applying fertiliser safely
lessons.html:
Applying fertiliser safely

Your team leader will tell you which fertiliser to use, how much and where. Always follow the instructions on the bag.

Before you start

  • Check the bag: is it the right fertiliser?
  • Get the measuring cup or scoop. Never guess the amount.
  • Wear gloves and closed shoes. Wear a dust mask if the fertiliser is dusty.
  • Water the plants the day before if the soil is very dry.

Granules on beds and shrubs

  1. Measure the amount for each plant or each square metre.
  2. Spread it evenly on the soil around the plant, out to the edge of the leaves. This is where the feeding roots are.
  3. Keep it off the stems and leaves.
  4. Scratch it lightly into the soil with a hand fork.
  5. Water well straight after. Water takes the food to the roots.

Lawns

  1. Use a spreader if you have one, set to the right amount.
  2. Walk in straight lines. Overlap a little so there are no gaps.
  3. Do not stop in one place with the spreader open. The grass will burn there.
  4. Water the lawn well after.

Liquid fertiliser

Mix the exact amount in water as the label says. Pour on the soil around the plant with a watering can. Rinse the can after.

Storing and cleaning up

  • Sweep up fertiliser from paths and paving.
  • Close bags and store them dry, off the floor, away from children and animals.
  • Wash your hands before you eat or drink.
  • If fertiliser gets in your eyes, rinse with clean water for a long time and tell your team leader.

Key points

  • N is for leaves, P for roots and flowers, K for plant health.
  • Always measure; never guess the amount.
  • Spread evenly, keep off stems and leaves.
  • Water well after applying.
  • Too much fertiliser burns plants and pollutes water.
